entities.name: Abul Hasan Ali
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Samarri, the last of the Four Deputies, played a pivotal role in the history of Shia Islam.

Born into the Samarrian family, a prominent clan of clerics and intellectuals in 9th-century Iraq, Ali succeeded Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Ruh al-Nawbakhti as the spiritual representative of the Hidden Imam Muhammad al-Mahdi in 937 CE. This marked the beginning of a 3-year period known as the Minor Occultation, during which Ali's role as the Deputy was not explicitly recognized by the Sunni authorities.

Ali's tenure was marked by significant theological and juridical developments, including the compilation of the Samarrian corpus of Shia jurisprudence, which would later become a foundational text for the Twelver Shia tradition. His leadership also facilitated the spread of Shia Islam throughout the Middle East and Central Asia, particularly in the regions of modern-day Iran, Iraq, and Afghanistan.

Ali's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as his successors continued to shape the Shia tradition and its institutions. His role as the last of the Four Deputies also highlights the complex and often contentious relationships between the Shia communities and their Sunni counterparts.

The significance of Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Samarri lies in his pivotal role in the history of Shia Islam, particularly during the Minor Occultation period. His leadership and theological innovations had a lasting impact on the development of Shia jurisprudence and the spread of Shia Islam in the Middle East and Central Asia.
